title: Watch Painted with a Pastoral Scene
medium: Outer case of painted enamel on gold. Inner case of gold with an unidentified maker's mark consisting of the letters ic over b below a coronet (incuse) on the interior and an eagle's head, a French guarantee mark for gold in use between 1 January 1847 and 1 July 1919 on the pendant. Dial of gold and white enamel with black numerals; silver hands set with diamond chips. Movement of gilt brass and steel. Movement signed (on the back plate): Tomson/london.

altText: A small gold pocket watch with a painted enamel outer case. The painted decoration is a countryside scene with people and musical instruments.

context: A watch made around 1758–65 with a gold case decorated in painted enamel. The Met lists its culture as French and probably Swiss, and its movement is signed Tomson/london, so it combines work from more than one place. The watch is about 6 centimeters high.

descriptions.k: This is a tiny watch, made long ago. Its gold case is covered with a painted picture of the countryside. There are people and music in the picture. What do you see? What song might they play?
descriptions.g12: This little watch is covered in a painted picture of the countryside. The case is gold with enamel, which is colored glass baked onto metal. The picture shows people with musical instruments. The watch is only about six centimeters tall. What story do you think the picture tells?
descriptions.g35: This watch was made around 1758 to 1765. Its gold case is decorated with painted enamel showing a pastoral scene, a peaceful picture of country life that includes people and musical instruments. Inside, the watch has a white enamel dial with black numbers and silver hands set with tiny diamond chips. The works are signed Tomson, London. Why might the maker decorate the outside so carefully?
descriptions.g68: This watch is a small package of craft: gold, painted enamel, white enamel dial, and a gilt brass and steel movement. The outer case shows a pastoral scene, a popular idea of peaceful country life, with musicians. The movement is signed Tomson, London, while the case is described as French and probably Swiss, which shows how parts and skills moved between countries. How does the painting make a timepiece feel like a treasure?
descriptions.g910: Around 1758 to 1765, a watch like this was both a measuring tool and a miniature painting. The pastoral scene on the gold and enamel case presents an idealized country life with musicians, a theme popular in eighteenth-century decorative arts. Meanwhile the movement is signed Tomson, London, even though the case is French and probably Swiss. Consider how the object brings together art, technology, and international trade.
descriptions.g1112: This watch complicates any simple national label. The Met describes the case as French and probably Swiss, the movement is signed Tomson, London, and a French gold guarantee mark dating from the nineteenth century indicates later handling. Its pastoral enamel scene belongs to a courtly taste for idealized rural life, but what any owner thought of it is not documented. How do hybrid objects like this affect our ideas about authorship, authenticity, and where a work of art comes from?

teacherNote.context: A watch from about 1758–65 with a painted enamel gold case, a signed London movement, and a later French gold mark. Which view the photograph shows is not specified in the record, so teachers should confirm what students can see.
directions: Ask students to design a painted scene for a round object and explain how the circle affects their composition.
Discuss how a signature on one part of an object can tell only part of its story.
Compare this watch with a modern phone case or watch face and discuss what we decorate and why.
